sheets.title: Test Plan
cells: A test plan helps you to test efficiently and to cover the most crucial aspects of the Information Technology (IT) you are testing.  Depending on the nature of the IT, you may focus on Sections testing or Functions testing

Sections testing: If you are testing informational websites, choose sections of pages that repeat frequently (like banner, footer). You may also need to include whole pages that are unique (like Homepage, or Search Results). See tutorial on how to choose sections.

Functions testing: If you are testing a dynamic website where you get to add, edit, delete information, change settings, etc. like MCommunity, it would make sense to list functions that you are testing. These would be things like "login", "change settings", "create a group" etc.  See tutorial on how to choose functions

You can add the two types of tests below in Column A.
Items listed there will automatically become options in the "Sections" column  of the "Findings: Issues" sheet. Currently listed are some placeholders with sections that many websites have, but you are encouraged to edit, add, or delete them to fit the website you are working on.

sheets.title: Summary
cells: This report has findings from a "baseline" level accessibility evaluation. This is a preliminary review on a limited sample. This is not a full WCAG conformance report.

Axcess scanned 5 pages of https://example.org/ on April 22, 2026. It found 51 issues to review: 45 where a rule check failed, and 6 that a person must confirm. Findings Issues has one row for each place an issue appears (an occurrence): 84 rows in all. Automated checks find only some accessibility problems, so test by hand as well.
Severity is a first estimate from the automated impact rating. No issue is marked Blocker, because that depends on which tasks are core to the site, which a person must judge. Confirm each issue and its severity before you share this report.

April 22, 2026, Axcess scan: Text does not stand out enough from its background (occurrence 1 of 3)
The rule check (axe) measured the contrast between the text color and its background color, and it is too low. Normal text needs a ratio of at least 4.5:1, and large text needs 3:1. Large text is at least 18pt (24px), or at least 14pt (about 18.7px) and bold. The rule check does not report text it cannot measure, such as text over an image or a gradient.
Page: Home: https://example.org/
Element locator (CSS selector): p > span.muted
What the check found: Fix any of the following: the rule's check failed.
Found by: Rule check (axe). How sure: Mostly sure. A rule check failed. Check it on the page to confirm.
How to fix:
• Open the occurrence and read the measured ratio, the two colors, the font size and the font weight. For example: "color contrast of 4.16 (foreground color: #3170fb, background color: #fafafc, font size: 9.0pt (12px), font weight: normal). Expected contrast ratio of 4.5:1". The foreground color is the text color.
• Put the two colors into a contrast checker, such as the WebAIM Contrast Checker. Find a darker text color or a lighter background that reaches 4.5:1, or 3:1 for large text. Do not round up: 4.499:1 does not pass.
• Change the color where the whole site sets it, such as a shared color setting (design token) or a CSS custom property like --link-color. One setting often colors many elements, so one change can fix many occurrences.
• Check the same text in every state people can see, such as hover, focus and visited.
People with any visual impairment may not be able to access information or content.

April 22, 2026, Axcess scan: Images have no alt text for screen readers (occurrence 1 of 1) An image () has no alt text (the text a screen reader reads for an image). The rule check (axe) found no alt attribute, aria-label, aria-labelledby or title, and no role that marks it as decoration (role="none" or role="presentation"). An alt that holds only a space, such as alt=" ", also fails. The check only sees whether alt text exists, not whether it is good. Page: Home: https://example.org/ Element locator (CSS selector): main > img.banner What the check found: Fix any of the following: the rule's check failed. Found by: Rule check (axe). How sure: Mostly sure. A rule check failed. Check it on the page to confirm. How to fix: • Decide what the image does on this page. If it gives information, write alt text that says what it means, not how it looks. For example, write "Acme logo", not "blue square with letters": . Do not use the file name or the word "image". • If the image is only decoration, add an empty alt: alt="", with nothing between the quotes. Screen readers then skip it. • An image that is the only content of a link or a button needs alt text that says what it does. For a link, say where it goes: . • Change the content management system (CMS) field or the page template so every image always gets an alt attribute, even an empty one.

April 22, 2026, Axcess scan: Form fields have no name for screen readers (occurrence 1 of 1)
A form field has no name that a screen reader can read (accessible name). The rule check (axe) looks at every <input> except buttons and hidden fields, and at every <textarea>. This field has no <label> with text around it or pointing to it, and no aria-label, aria-labelledby, title or placeholder. A label hidden from screen readers does not count, and drop-down lists (<select>) have their own rule (select-name).
Page: Contact: https://example.org/contact
Element locator (CSS selector): input[type=text]
What the check found: Fix any of the following: the rule's check failed.
Found by: Rule check (axe). How sure: Mostly sure. A rule check failed. Check it on the page to confirm.
How to fix:
• Add a visible label and tie it to the field: <label for="email">Email</label> <input id="email" type="email">. The for value must match the field's id exactly. A visible label helps everyone, not only screen reader users.
• Or wrap the field in its label: <label><input type="checkbox"> Send me updates</label>.
• If a <label> element does not fit, name the field another way. Give text already on screen an id and point to it with aria-labelledby="that-id", or add aria-label="Search" to the field.
• Do not use placeholder as the only label. It passes this rule check, but it disappears when the person starts typing. Browsers also usually show it in a pale color that does not meet the WCAG contrast minimum.
Status in Axcess: Accepted risk.

April 22, 2026, Axcess scan: Some content sits outside any page region (occurrence 1 of 2)
The rule check (axe) found content outside every landmark. A landmark is a page region that screen reader users can jump to, such as the menu (<nav>) or the main content (<main>). A few things may sit outside, such as skip links, dialogs and areas that announce updates (live regions, aria-live). WCAG does not require this, but it is a best practice.
Page: https://example.org/products
Element locator (CSS selector): div.promo
What the check found: Fix any of the following: the rule's check failed.
Found by: Rule check (axe). How sure: Mostly sure. A rule check failed. Check it on the page to confirm.
How to fix:
• Use the element locator (CSS selector) in an occurrence to find the content. Look at its parent elements in the browser's developer tools to see which part of the layout it belongs to.
• Put each part of the page into the matching landmark. Use <header> for the top of the site and <nav> for menus. Use <main> for the page's own content, <aside> for side content and <footer> for the footer. Use only one <main> per page. For example: <body><header>…</header><main>…</main><footer>…</footer></body>
• Fix it in the shared page template or layout component. The rule check (axe) reports each block of content separately. So one missing wrapper can cause many occurrences, and one template change can clear them all.
Screen reader users often open a list of landmarks and jump between them. Content outside every landmark is not in that list, so they can miss it or not know what it belongs to.

A few things may sit outside, such as skip links, dialogs and areas that announce updates (live regions, aria-live). WCAG does not require this, but it is a best practice.
Page: Blog: https://example.org/blog
Element locator (CSS selector): div.promo
What the check found: Fix any of the following: the rule's check failed.
Found by: Rule check (axe). How sure: Mostly sure. A rule check failed. Check it on the page to confirm.
How to fix:
• Use the element locator (CSS selector) in an occurrence to find the content. Look at its parent elements in the browser's developer tools to see which part of the layout it belongs to.
• Put each part of the page into the matching landmark. Use <header> for the top of the site and <nav> for menus. Use <main> for the page's own content, <aside> for side content and <footer> for the footer. Use only one <main> per page. For example: <body><header>…</header><main>…</main><footer>…</footer></body>
• Fix it in the shared page template or layout component. The rule check (axe) reports each block of content separately. So one missing wrapper can cause many occurrences, and one template change can clear them all.
Screen reader users often open a list of landmarks and jump between them. Content outside every landmark is not in that list, so they can miss it or not know what it belongs to.

April 22, 2026, Axcess scan: Text misses the stricter Level AAA contrast ratio (occurrence 1 of 1)
The rule check (axe) found text that meets the Level AA contrast minimum but not the stricter Level AAA level. The contrast ratio measures how much lighter one color is than the other, from 1:1 (same color) to 21:1 (black on white). This text is at least 4.5:1 but under 7:1, or, for large text, at least 3:1 but under 4.5:1. Text below the AA minimum shows up in the color-contrast issue instead.
Page: About us: https://example.org/about
Element locator (CSS selector): p.subtle
What the check found: Fix any of the following: the rule's check failed.
Found by: Rule check (axe). How sure: Mostly sure. A rule check failed. Check it on the page to confirm.
How to fix:
• Check whether your policy asks for Level AAA. If it asks only for Level AA, you do not have to fix this, but a fix still helps people with low vision. The World Wide Web Consortium (W3C), which writes WCAG, does not advise requiring Level AAA for a whole site. Some content cannot meet every Level AAA criterion.
• Open each occurrence and read the check's message. It gives the contrast ratio, the text color (foreground color), the background color, the font size and the font weight. For example: "contrast of 6.54 ... Expected contrast ratio of 7:1".
• Pick a darker text color, or a lighter background, that reaches 7:1 for normal text, or 4.5:1 for large text. Large text is 24px (18pt) or bigger, or 14pt (about 18.7px) or bigger in bold. Do not round up: 6.99:1 does not meet 7:1. For example, on white, #767676 gives 4.54:1 and #595959 just reaches 7:1.
• Change the color in the shared style (the design token or CSS custom property, such as --text-muted: #595959;), not on each element. One shared color often causes many occurrences, so one change can fix them all.

Text that blends into its background is hard to read for people with low vision, and color blindness can lower the contrast even more. The 7:1 level makes up for the contrast loss of about 20/80 vision (seeing at 20 feet what most people see at 80 feet).

The keyboard check presses Tab through the page, up to about 100 times. It reports an element when focus stays on it through 4 more presses of Tab and then 4 presses of Shift+Tab. Normal cases do not count, such as focus going back to the top, moving between two controls, or staying in a pop-up window (modal dialog). The check also skips parts it cannot see inside. • Open the live page and press Tab until you reach the element in the element locator (CSS selector). Then press Tab and Shift+Tab several times each, and watch where focus goes.

How to fix:
• Measure the control in the browser developer tools, and note which side is under 44 pixels.
• Make the clickable area at least 44 by 44 pixels, for example .icon-button { display: inline-block; min-width: 44px; min-height: 44px; }. Padding inside the control adds to the area; margin outside it does not.
